lessons.title: recordar — to remember, and to remind
lessons.gloss: to remember, to remind — to pass a thing back through the heart

segments.text: Say el corazón and la cita. The heart is inside the verb that keeps the appointment.
recordar — to remember, and also to remind.
No recuerdo su nombre — I don't remember his name. Recuérdame la cita — remind me about the appointment. Te recuerdo que mañana es fiesta — I remind you that tomorrow is a holiday.
One verb, both jobs. Which it is depends on whether somebody else is being told: recuerdo alone is remembering, te recuerdo is reminding.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: recordar is not acordarse

segments.text: Spanish has a second verb for remembering and the two are near-twins:

utterances: Spanish: recordar algo. what it takes: a plain object.
Spanish: acordarse de algo. what it takes: de, always.

segments.text: No recuerdo la dirección and no me acuerdo de la dirección mean the same thing. The difference is grammatical, not semantic: recordar takes the thing directly, acordarse needs its de, and dropping it is one of the commonest mistakes learners make.
Both are o becomes ue verbs: recuerdo, me acuerdo. The same break you have been tracking since la rueda.
Latin recordari: re-, back, plus cor, cordis — the heart.
To remember is to bring back through the heart, because Latin located memory and thought there rather than in the head. That is the same cor inside el corazón, which you have had for many chapters.

The family is everywhere once seen: el acuerdo, an agreement — hearts brought together — and recordar's English cousin record, which is literally a thing committed to memory. Courage is cor too, by way of French, and so is concordance.
So a Spanish speaker asking you to remember something is asking you to run it back past your heart.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: I don't remember the appointment]

segments.text: To remember? (Recordar.) I remember? (Recuerdo.) What is cor? (The heart — the same one in corazón.)

lessons.title: el dentista / la dentista — the dentist
lessons.gloss: the dentist — an -ista noun, where only the article changes

segments.text: Say el diente and el médico. Put them together and name the person.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: el dentista

segments.text: el dentista, la dentista — the dentist.
Tengo cita con el dentista — I've got a dentist's appointment. Voy al dentista — I'm going to the dentist's.
Note al dentista for the place as well as the person: Spanish sends you to the professional, not to the surgery, where English says "to the dentist's".

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: -ista does not change for gender

segments.text: -ista nouns have one form for both, and only the article moves:

utterances: the person: dentist. masculine: el dentista. feminine: la dentista.
the person: artist. masculine: el artista. feminine: la artista.
the person: tourist. masculine: el turista. feminine: la turista.

segments.text: The -a ending misleads, because it looks feminine and is not. El dentista is correct and el dentisto does not exist.

Compare el médico / la médica, which does change. The difference is the ending: -ista is invariable, -o is not. Learn the ending and the article stops being a guess — the same bargain the noun-making suffixes offered.
Latin dens, dentem — tooth — plus the Greek ending -istēs, which names somebody who does a thing.

So dentista is a Latin body part with a Greek job-ending welded on, which is how most modern profession words were built: el periodista, el electricista, el taxista. The ending is productive, meaning Spanish still makes new ones.
Dentem gives el diente, and English dental, dentist and indent — to cut a tooth-shaped notch. A dandelion is dent de lion, a lion's tooth, named for its leaves.

lessons.title: fallar — to fail somebody
lessons.gloss: to fail, to let somebody down — the deceiving inside falso

segments.text: Say falso and estropeado. One is about truth, one about machines. The verb next covers both.
fallar — to fail, to go wrong, to let somebody down.
Me falló el coche — the car let me down. Ha fallado el sistema — the system has gone down. No me falles — don't let me down.
El fallo is the noun: a fault, a glitch, and in an exam a wrong answer.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: fallar is not estropearse

segments.text: Both are about things going wrong, and they are not the same:

utterances: what happened: it stopped working, and stayed that way. the verb: estropearse.
what happened: it did not do its job at the moment needed. the verb: fallar.

segments.text: Se ha estropeado el coche — it is broken, in the garage. Me falló el coche — it let me down, this morning, when I needed it. A car can fallar once and be fine afterwards.
That is why fallar is the verb for people too. Me falló about a friend is a reproach: they were not there when it counted.
Latin fallere, to deceive — and that is the same verb inside falso, which you already have.

The move from deceiving to failing runs through disappointment: something that fails you has, in effect, misled you about what it would do. Latin fallere already carried both, and Spanish kept the pair — falso for the lie, fallar for the letting-down.
English took it twice as well: false from the participle, and fail through French. Fault, fallacy and failure are all here, and so is default, which is a failing to act.
A second Spanish branch is faltar, to be lacking — me falta tiempo, I'm short of time — from the same root by a different road.

lessons.title: (recordar, el dentista, fallar) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the three, and two words that were already in your vocabulary

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: to remember, the dentist, to let down.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two bodies and a lie

utterances: new word: recordar. what it was built on: cor, the heart — the one in el corazón.
new word: el dentista. what it was built on: dentem, a tooth — the one in el diente.
new word: fallar. what it was built on: fallere, to deceive — the one in falso.

segments.text: Two body parts and a lie, and all three were already in your vocabulary. By this stage that is the ordinary case rather than a happy accident: a corpus of nine hundred words contains most of the roots the next hundred will need.
Recordar is the one worth keeping. Latin put memory in the heart, not the head, so remembering is running a thing back past it — and English record is the same word, a thing committed to memory.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: endings that fix the article, and one that does not

utterances: ending: -ista. what it settles: nothing changes; only the article moves.
ending: -o / -a. what it settles: the noun itself changes: el médico, la médica.

segments.text: El dentista looks feminine and is not. That -a is Greek, not the Spanish feminine, which is why the noun stays put and the article does the work.

lessons.title: (perder la cita) — read it, then do it yourself
lessons.gloss: the payoff — read a reminder and the apology for missing it, then write both

segments.text: Say recordar and fallar. The first message does one; the second admits the other.
Two messages, a day apart. Read both, then answer.
1 — de la clínica.
Le recordamos su cita con la dentista el jueves a las 10:15. Para anular, llame con 24 horas de antelación.
2 — el jueves por la tarde.
Buenas tardes. Siento no haber ido esta mañana; me falló el despertador y no me acordé hasta las once. ¿Puedo pedir otra cita?

segments.text: The apology uses both verbs for remembering and they are doing different work. Me falló el despertador — the alarm clock is the subject; it let the writer down. Then no me acordé — acordarse, the reflexive one, for the person's own failure to recall. Spanish separates the thing that failed from the person who forgot, and the apology is more honest for it.

La dentista, feminine, so the clinic is naming a particular woman. And con la dentista, not con el dentista — had the message said el, you would know it was a man, since the noun itself never tells you.
Siento no haber ido is the standard apology frame: sentir plus a perfect infinitive. Not siento que no fui, which a learner reaches for and a Spanish speaker does not.

Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines: as the clinic, remind somebody of a dental appointment and say how to cancel; then as the patient, apologise for missing it, say what let you down, and ask for another.
Then check yourself: did fallar go to the thing and acordarse to the person, and did acordarse keep its de?
